title: The Referral Cut

options.B: Fulfilled by Amazon (FBA) -- Mia hands fulfillment over to Amazon's own warehouses

_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC SS4
protagonist: Mia Torres, owner-operator of Amber & Oak (small-batch soy candles)

deliverables.text: A referral-fee conversion: convert Appendix B's published referral fee percentage into an exact fraction in lowest terms, and use it to find the referral retention fraction -- the fraction of the sale price Mia actually keeps after Amazon's referral fee, before any other cost is considered. Then multiply Appendix A's list price (a mixed number of dollars) by the referral retention fraction to find Mia's post-referral proceeds -- the amount both options start from before their own separate further costs are subtracted.

Option A (FBM)'s true net margin per unit: subtract Appendix A's per-unit packaging-and-postage cost and per-unit production cost (both mixed numbers) from D1's post-referral proceeds -- all in fraction and mixed-number arithmetic, no decimals at any step.

Option B (FBA)'s true total per-unit fulfillment fee: convert Appendix C's fuel-and-logistics surcharge percentage into an exact fraction, and multiply Appendix C's base per-unit fulfillment fee (as a fraction of a dollar) by one plus that surcharge fraction -- fraction times fraction -- to find the true total fee Amazon actually deducts per unit under Option B. Show why multiplying the base fee by (1 + the surcharge fraction) is not the same operation as simply adding the surcharge's raw percentage number onto the base fee's dollar amount, and which of the two actually reflects how Amazon applies the surcharge.

Option B's true net margin per unit, found by subtracting D3's total per-unit fulfillment fee and Appendix A's per-unit production cost from D1's post-referral proceeds -- then, for both options, multiply each option's net margin per unit (D2 and D4) by Appendix A's guaranteed monthly order quantity, a whole number, to find each option's total monthly net margin, and state which option wins and by how much.

A working-capital comparison: for each option, multiply Appendix A's stated weeks of finished inventory that option requires Mia to hold (a mixed number) by Appendix A's weekly production cost (a mixed number) to find how many dollars of unsold inventory each option ties up at any given moment -- two separate mixed-number-by-mixed-number calculations, one per option.

An original visual display comparing, side by side, each option's total monthly net margin (from D4) against the dollars of working capital it ties up (from D5) -- built from your own D4 and D5 figures, with every dollar amount on the display labeled as an exact mixed number, never rounded to a decimal.

balance.argument_a: FBM's real, quantitative case: Mia pays no fulfillment fee to Amazon at all -- only the 15% referral fee [S1] -- and her own $3-1/8 packaging/postage cost is one she controls directly, unlike a marketplace fee schedule she cannot negotiate. Post-referral proceeds are $15-15/16 per unit; after her own $3-1/8 packaging/postage cost and $6-1/2 production cost, her true net margin is $6-5/16/unit, or $252-1/2/month at Rivendell's guaranteed 40-unit order -- the higher of the two options. Its real weakness is working capital: Appendix A's 6-1/2 weeks of held, unsold inventory (versus Option B's 2-1/4 weeks) ties up real cash every month that can't be spent on next month's wax, wicks, and jars.
balance.argument_b: FBA's real, quantitative case: its combined fee -- referral fee [S1] plus a true total per-unit fulfillment fee of $3.68 x 1.035 [S2, S3] -- replaces a cost Mia already pays herself under FBM (packaging + postage), and frees up several weeks' worth of working capital that FBM leaves sitting on a shelf as unsold inventory (2-1/4 weeks tied up under B versus 6-1/2 under A). Its true net margin is $5-6287/10000/unit, or $225-37/250/month -- genuinely lower than FBM's by a real, computed 10.83%, not a paper number: Amazon's fulfillment fee plus its 2026 fuel-and-logistics surcharge [S3] currently costs Mia more per unit than the packaging/postage she already pays herself, even though it is real, sourced, and non-negotiable.
balance.margin_basis: margin = |monthly_net_margin(A) - monthly_net_margin(B)| / max(monthly_net_margin(A), monthly_net_margin(B)), where monthly_net_margin(option) = net_margin_per_unit(option) x 40 units (Appendix A's guaranteed monthly order quantity). post_referral_proceeds = 18-3/4 x 17/20 = 15-15/16 (D1). net_margin_per_unit(A) = 15-15/16 - 3-1/8 (packaging) - 6-1/2 (production) = 6-5/16. total_fulfillment_fee(B) = 3.68 x (1 + 7/200) = 3.8088 (D3). net_margin_per_unit(B) = 15-15/16 - 3.8088 - 6-1/2 = 5.6287. monthly_A = 6-5/16 x 40 = 252-1/2. monthly_B = 5.6287 x 40 = 225.148. margin = |252.5 - 225.148| / 252.5 = 10.83%. Within the approved concept's 8-15% target band. A (FBM) wins under the current sourced figures -- computed exactly in sensitivity_model.py using Python's Fraction class throughout, no floating-point rounding at any intermediate step.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: Amber & Oak's own per-unit packaging/postage cost (Appendix A) is the case author's own chosen operational figure, not an externally verifiable fact about a real named entity -- nobody outside the fictional business could source or falsify it. It plays the same epistemic role a stated Modeling Assumption plays elsewhere in this corpus even though case.md presents it as ordinary given data rather than in a Modeling Assumptions block (this case needed no such block -- all three real Amazon fee figures were genuinely SOURCED, see RESEARCH_LOG.md). Tier 2 P5 (sensitivity_model.py, FLEX=['packaging_cost']) found the verdict flips from A to B at a +50% flex ($4.6875/unit vs. the base $3.125/unit); the exact flip point is $3.8088/unit, a real, computed threshold, not disclosed as a number in case.md or FACILITATOR.md's Twist section per the no-leaked-answer rule -- only the direction and existence of the sensitivity is disclosed there.
